newsitem.title: COSTA RICA: Ozone summit sets target for destroying chemicals.
newsitem.headline: Ozone summit sets target for destroying chemicals.

text.p: Delegates from 164 countries at a world Ozone Summit agreed on Wednesday to spend $540 million to destroy 21,000 tonnes of ozone-eating chemicals in the next three years.

In a final statement at the end of a three-day meeting in San Jose, delegates said the money would come from a multilateral fund set up in 1987 to help developing nations switch to the use of less environmentally damaging chemicals.
The Costa Rican meeting brought together signatories of the 1987 Montreal Protocol and the 1985 Vienna Convention.

The protocol, ratified by at least 150 countries, called for the gradual phasing out of ozone-depleting substances and established the multilateral fund to encourage technology transfer and the switch to less harmful substances.
The convention set up a framework for reducing production of chemicals that deplete the ozone layer, including chlorofluorocarbons, which are widely used in refrigeration and aerosols.

The approximately 800 delegates earlier heard a report from the United Nations' World Meteorological Organisation that said the hole in the ozone layer over the South Pole reached its largest size in history in 1996.

"In the second half of September and the beginning of October of 1996, the size of the ozone hole in Antarctica surpassed 22 million square kilometres (8.5 million square miles)," G.O.P. Obasi, secretary-general of the WMO, told delegates.
The size of the hole is equivalent to twice the surface of Europe from the Atlantic Ocean to the Ural Mountains.
Ozone depletion increases the Earth's exposure to harmful ultraviolet radiation, which has been linked to skin cancer in humans.

In the closing statement, representatives of industrialised nations pledged to contribute to the multilateral fund and act to protect the ozone layer, while the Group of 77 developing countries and China promised to use the money effectively to reduce ozone depletion.
"If the decisions foreseen here are carried out, the situation may improve by halfway through the next century," Sam Ongeri, president of the Montreal Protocol group, told reporters.
The multilateral fund has already been used to eliminate more than 75,000 tonnes of ozone-depleting chemicals in the last three years at a cost of $530 million, delegates heard.
Delegates also agreed on a 1997 quota for producing ozone-depleting chemicals for essential uses in the industrialised world.
"A total of 13,000 tonnes of substances harmful to the ozone layer has been approved for 1997," the closing statement said.
"The amounts for 1998 to 2001 are subject to annual revision by a panel of economic and technical experts and to approval by the parties," the statement said.
